description: This research report examines India’s emerging AI power through the interaction of usable national capacity, technological dependence, boundary control, strategic autonomy, and cognitive security. It argues that India’s position is best understood as a distributed and vertically uneven mixed-control system: strong software capacity, digital public infrastructure, multilingual public technology, a large technical workforce, expanding compute access, and globally distributed technical networks coexist with dependence on externally controlled upstream technologies. The report distinguishes access from mobilizable capability, territorial presence from control, boundary power from boundary autonomy, and systemic influence from narrower bilateral effects. It concludes that India’s long-term AI power will depend on conversion, substitutability, resilient public infrastructure, selective boundary control, and the ability to preserve agency without full technological autarky.
abstract: This research report examines India’s emerging AI power through the interaction of usable national capacity, technological dependence, boundary control, strategic autonomy, and cognitive security. Rather than treating AI power as equivalent to frontier-model performance, compute scale, or investment volume, it analyzes how technical, institutional, organizational, and infrastructural capabilities are converted into nationally usable power under conditions of uneven interdependence. India is used as a mechanism-rich case because substantial software capacity, digital public infrastructure, multilingual public technology, expanding compute access, and globally distributed technical networks coexist with continued dependence on externally controlled upstream technologies. The report distinguishes access from mobilizable capability, territorial presence from control, boundary power from boundary autonomy, and persistent systemic influence from narrower bilateral effects. It also examines how procurement, regulation, interoperability, substitution, and institutional conversion shape India’s ability to preserve agency without requiring full technological autarky. The report is based on publicly available evidence through August 31, 2026 and is intended as a theory-guided analytical study rather than a national AI ranking or predictive assessment.

methodology.framework_name: AI Power, Boundary Autonomy, and Cognitive-Security Conversion Framework
methodology.source_basis: Theory-guided single-country analytical case study based on publicly available legal, regulatory, parliamentary, central-bank, ministry, corporate first-party, peer-reviewed, industry, and high-quality news sources through August 31, 2026.
methodology.case_context: India’s emerging AI power in a distributed and vertically uneven technological order, with attention to IndiaAI, BHASHINI, semiconductor conversion, Global Capability Centres, payment-data localization, India Stack, UPI, MOSIP, AI governance, and cognitive security.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is how India can build, exercise, and preserve AI-related agency when ownership, infrastructure, knowledge, and technological control are distributed across national and transnational systems.
central_claims: India’s AI power is vertically uneven rather than simply high or low.
Access to AI resources does not equal nationally usable power.

India’s strongest capabilities lie downstream and institutionally: software integration, GCCs, digital public infrastructure, public administration, multilingual AI, and a population-scale domestic market.

India remains dependent on externally controlled upstream technologies including advanced accelerators, semiconductor equipment, EDA, high-performance memory, cloud-management layers, and parts of the frontier-model ecosystem.
India’s strongest demonstrated boundary power lies in interfaces where Indian institutions possess enforceable jurisdiction or participation control.
Payment-data localization provides the clearest demonstrated effective ABP case.
Strategic autonomy under AI interdependence is better understood as selective autonomy and boundary autonomy than full technological autarky.
India’s DPI and MOSIP experience suggests that institutional architecture can diffuse internationally without India retaining control over foreign systems.
India’s AI-specific systemic influence remains emerging, while adjacent DPI influence is more mature.

Cognitive security requires multilingual verification, provenance, authentication, continuity, substitutability, redundant infrastructure, protected language resources, privacy, due process, proportionality, contestability, and oversight.

analytical_lenses.name: Usable National Capacity
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses AI-relevant capabilities that the Indian national system can actually mobilize and sustain.

analytical_lenses.name: AI Boundary Power
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses relational ability to alter the conditions under which other actors access, transfer, integrate, deploy, or use a resource or function.

analytical_lenses.name: Boundary Autonomy
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses India’s ability to switch, bypass, substitute, diversify, or selectively internalize when another actor controls a critical interface.

analytical_lenses.name: Systemic Influence
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses persistent and sufficiently broad effects across networks, rules, or future participation conditions.

analytical_lenses.name: Conversion
analytical_lenses.description: Tracks how distributed resources across ownership, geography, and organizational boundaries become usable national capability.

analytical_lenses.name: Attribution Discipline
analytical_lenses.description: Separates nationally mobilizable capacity from the wider India-linked technological footprint.

analytical_lenses.name: Cognitive-Security Stress Test
analytical_lenses.description: Uses an illustrative information-shock scenario to evaluate integrity, provenance, authentication, multilingual capability, continuity, substitutability, and interface governance.

dimensions.name: Territorial-Infrastructural Capacity
dimensions.description: Data centers, IndiaAI shared compute, NIC/MeghRaj, cloud regions, network proximity, and domestic hosting capacity.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Installed data-center capacity rose from about 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW by August 2026; IndiaAI shared capacity exceeded 45,000 GPUs by June 2026.
dimensions.interpretation: India’s territorial AI infrastructure is expanding, but India-located capacity does not equal sovereign compute or crisis-time substitutability.

dimensions.name: Human-Epistemic Capacity
dimensions.description: Engineers, semiconductor designers, universities, expert communities, and global professional networks.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Government reporting cited industry estimates that India employed nearly 20% of the global semiconductor chip-design workforce and hosted about 7% of semiconductor-domain GCCs.
dimensions.interpretation: Large knowledge depth exists, but identity, location, or workforce share does not establish IP ownership or national mobilizability.

dimensions.name: Economic-Industrial Capacity
dimensions.description: Software/IT services, Global Capability Centres, startups, domestic demand, and semiconductor projects.
dimensions.observed_pattern: India’s GCC sector was estimated at 2,117 centres, about 2.36 million professionals, and US$98.4 billion expected revenue in FY2025–26.
dimensions.interpretation: India has a large downstream conversion layer, but foreign-parent control and client orientation create mixed control.

dimensions.name: Political-Administrative Mobilization
dimensions.description: IndiaAI, compute subsidy, public AI pipeline, procurement, regulation, and implementation institutions.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Government-wide exercise identified 762 AI problem statements; IndiaAI progress summary reported 62 prototypes and 20 deployments.
dimensions.interpretation: Administrative conversion is visible, but discovery pipelines, prototypes, and deployed systems should not be treated as a single conversion funnel.

dimensions.name: Cultural-Linguistic Fit
dimensions.description: Multilingual society, language resources, and public-language AI infrastructure.
dimensions.observed_pattern: BHASHINI supported 36 Indian text languages and 23 Indian voice languages, powered more than 800 government websites, and processed more than 24 million AI inferences per day.
dimensions.interpretation: Multilingual diversity becomes an AI-power asset only when institutional infrastructure can operate across it.

dimensions.name: Payment-Data Localization
dimensions.description: RBI payment-data localization, audit, onboarding restriction, target compliance, and restored access.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Restrictions were imposed on payment firms for non-compliance and Mastercard access was restored after satisfactory compliance.
dimensions.interpretation: This is the clearest demonstrated effective state ABP case in the report.

dimensions.name: IndiaAI Procurement Boundary
dimensions.description: IndiaAI compute empanelment, pricing, service rules, provider obligations, SLAs, and user allocation.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Empanelled cloud service providers serve approved users under rules for hardware/software compatibility, accessibility, uptime, and provisioning.
dimensions.interpretation: Demonstrates an AI-specific operational gate but not payment-style coercive bargaining leverage.

dimensions.name: Synthetic-Generated Information Rules
dimensions.description: Duties for defined synthetic audio, visual, and audio-visual media, including labeling, metadata/identifier, and intermediary due diligence.
dimensions.observed_pattern: 2026 duties were established, but no payment-like enforcement or realized platform-response sequence is shown through the evidence cutoff.
dimensions.interpretation: Formal boundary authority exists; effective ABP and realized effects remain unassessed.

dimensions.name: Boundary Autonomy
dimensions.description: Switching, substitution, diversification, fallback, workload portability, provider choice, redesign, and selective internalization.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Provider diversity and routine compute allocation exist, but severe upstream disruption continuity is not publicly demonstrated.
dimensions.interpretation: India has stronger substitutability at service-provider and institutional layers than at frontier-hardware layers.

dimensions.name: Systemic Influence
dimensions.description: Persistent and sufficiently broad changes across networks, rules, or future participation conditions.
dimensions.observed_pattern: MOSIP and UPI show stronger adjacent-DPI diffusion; AI governance and standards influence remain earlier-stage.
dimensions.interpretation: India’s AI-specific systemic influence remains emerging rather than established at broad scale.

dimensions.name: Cognitive Security
dimensions.description: Integrity, provenance, authentication, multilingual capability, continuity, substitutability, and interface governance under AI-mediated information shock.
dimensions.observed_pattern: India has multilingual, compute, public-digital, regulatory, and Responsible AI components, but integrated nationwide performance under compound shock is not demonstrated.
dimensions.interpretation: Cognitive resilience is both a technical and institutional problem.

key_findings: India’s AI power is vertically uneven: strong software, DPI, multilingual AI, technical talent, and expanding compute coexist with dependence on externally controlled upstream technologies.

Access does not equal usable power: IndiaAI shows that externally sourced compute can be converted into nationally organized capability through procurement, subsidy, allocation, and service rules without transferring ownership of the underlying technology.
Boundary power is strongest where India controls participation conditions, including payments regulation, public procurement, platform rules, and interoperability.

Strategic autonomy does not require full technological self-sufficiency; the more realistic objective is preserving switching, substitution, diversification, fallback, and selective internalization at critical interfaces.

Digital public infrastructure can diffuse without creating foreign control; India’s DPI and MOSIP experience suggests that open and customizable architectures can extend institutional influence while leaving operational ownership with adopting states.

Cognitive resilience depends on both technology and governance, combining multilingual verification, provenance, continuity, alternative providers, protected public infrastructure, privacy, contestability, due process, and oversight.
India’s long-term AI advantage will depend on conversion from technical access and distributed capabilities into durable, governable, and resilient national capacity.
The report separates nationally mobilizable capacity from the wider India-linked technological footprint to avoid attributing overseas or foreign-controlled capability to India without evidence.
India’s semiconductor position shows knowledge and design depth, but upstream dependencies in fabrication, EDA, equipment, advanced memory, and accelerator supply remain consequential.
AI-specific systemic influence remains less mature than adjacent DPI influence.
policy_recommendations: Protect critical continuity and increase substitutability at externally controlled chokepoints.
Identify critical public workloads and specify minimum service levels, provider concentration limits, data/model exportability, fallback compute, migration time, and recovery objectives.
Deepen high-value conversion where India already has a large human and organizational base.
Track whether semiconductor design capability becomes owned IP, validated products, production, packaging, equipment/material competence, and resilient supplier relationships.
Evaluate GCC development by product ownership, R&D mandates, senior technical responsibility, and AI architecture rather than headcount alone.
Exercise and diffuse interface power only where evidence supports credible control or institutional attraction.
Distinguish formal rules from enforced target response and distinguish MoUs from operational foreign deployment.
Use open architectures to generate interoperability and institutional embeddedness without overstating foreign control.
Preserve privacy, due process, proportionality, appeal, contestability, and independent oversight in cognitive-security systems.

disclaimer: This research report presents a theory-guided analytical assessment of India’s emerging AI power, technological dependence, boundary control, strategic autonomy, and cognitive security. The frameworks, classifications, and case interpretations developed in this report are intended as analytical and diagnostic tools. They should not be interpreted as definitive measures of national power, deterministic predictions, comprehensive assessments of technological sovereignty, or official evaluations of any government, firm, institution, or technology provider. Empirical claims are based on publicly available information and remain subject to source limitations, reporting gaps, changing institutional conditions, and further verification.
